Predicting Blood Pressure: Linear, Polynomial and Kernel Regression

This analysis uses NHANES data that exists in a package for R.

NHANES consists of survey data collected by the US National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) which has conducted a series of health and nutrition surveys since the early 1960’s. Since 1999 approximately 5,000 individuals of all ages are interviewed in their homes every year and complete the health examination component of the survey. The health examination is conducted in a mobile examination center (MEC).

Note that there is the following warning on the NHANES website: “For NHANES datasets, the use of sampling weights and sample design variables is recommended for all analyses because the sample design is a clustered design and incorporates differential probabilities of selection. If you fail to account for the sampling parameters, you may obtain biased estimates and overstate significance levels.”

Here I ignore this warning and apply the analyses to the data as if they were randomly sampled! We will be using the data called NHANESraw.

For questions that ask for your comments, it suffices to answer with one or two sentences in each case.

Data Preparation

  1. Install the package NHANES into R, load the NHANES package, and then run the command data(NHANES) which will load the NHANES data. Type ?NHANES and read about the dataset.
install.packages("NHANES")
## 
## The downloaded binary packages are in
##  /var/folders/63/klpq6sss15lb697997qxym8m0000gn/T//Rtmpe56jcu/downloaded_packages
library(NHANES)
data(NHANES)
?NHANES
  1. Make an object nhanes that is a subset version NHANESraw that does not include any missing data for Diabetes, BPSysAve, BPDiaAve
df <- subset(NHANESraw, !is.na(Diabetes) & (!is.na(BPSysAve) & !is.na(BPDiaAve)))
  1. Plot BPSysAve against BPDiaAve. Comment on what is going on. Further subset the data such the observations with BPDiaAve equal to zero are removed.
plot( df$BPDiaAve, df$BPSysAve, main = "BPSysAve vs. BPDiaAve", xlab = "BPDiaAve", ylab = "BPSysAve", 
     cex = 0.3, col = adjustcolor("black", alpha.f = 0.5))

# There appears to be a positive linear relationship between BPSysAve and 
# BPDiaAve with points clustering around BPSyAve values between 100-150. 

df <- subset(df, BPDiaAve != 0)
plot(df$BPDiaAve, df$BPSysAve, main = "BPSysAve vs. BPDiaAve no zeros", xlab = "BPDiaAve", ylab = "BPDiaAve",
     cex = 0.3, col = adjustcolor("black", alpha.f = 0.5))

# There still appears to be a positive linear relationship between BPSysAve and 
# BPDiaAve with points clustering around BPSyAve values between 100-150.
  1. Make an object nhanes09 that is a subset of nhanes to only the 2009_10 data. This will be your training dataset. Also make an object nhanes11 that is a subset of nhanes to only the 2011_12 data. This will be your test dataset.
nhanes09 <- subset(df, SurveyYr == "2009_10")
nhanes11 <- subset(df, SurveyYr== "2011_12")

Linear regression

  1. Plot BPSysAve against BPDiaAve for the training data.
plot( nhanes09$BPDiaAve, nhanes09$BPSysAve, main = "BPSysAve vs. BPDiaAve 2009_10", xlab = "BPDiaAve", ylab = "BPSysAve",
     cex = 0.3, col = adjustcolor("black", alpha.f = 0.5))

  1. Fit a linear model using the training data with BPSysAve as outcome and BPDiaAve as the single predictor.
training_model <- lm(BPSysAve ~ BPDiaAve, data = nhanes09)
  1. Use the summary command to examine the resulting fitted model.
summary(training_model)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = BPSysAve ~ BPDiaAve, data = nhanes09)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -43.426 -11.253  -2.944   7.851 102.229 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept) 79.20945    0.91511   86.56   <2e-16 ***
## BPDiaAve     0.58634    0.01361   43.09   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 16.61 on 7723 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.1938, Adjusted R-squared:  0.1937 
## F-statistic:  1857 on 1 and 7723 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
  1. Generate 95% confidence intervals for the parameters of the fitted model.
confint(training_model, level = 0.95)
##                  2.5 %    97.5 %
## (Intercept) 77.4155794 81.003324
## BPDiaAve     0.5596641  0.613008
  1. Also, generate 99% confidence intervals for the parameters of the fitted model.
confint(training_model, level = 0.99)
##                0.5 %     99.5 %
## (Intercept) 76.85169 81.5672131
## BPDiaAve     0.55128  0.6213921
  1. Comment on the difference between the 95% and 99% confidence intervals and whether or not the difference is what you would expect.

The estimated intercept was 79.20945 (95% CI: 77.41557 - 81.00332, 99% CI: 76.8516 - 81.56721) and the estimated slope was 0.58634 (95% CI:0.55966 - 0.61300, 99% CI: 0.55128 - 0.6213921). The 99% CI is wider than the 95% CI and does reflect the expected difference as a 99% CI is meant to capture the true value with greater confidence, requiring a wider interval.

  1. Now fit models with quadratic and cubic terms in the predictor BPDiaAve in addition to the linear term. Look at the output of each model with summary and generate 95% confidence intervals for each.
qtm <- lm(BPSysAve ~ BPDiaAve + I(BPDiaAve^2), data = nhanes09)
ctm <- lm(BPSysAve ~ BPDiaAve + I(BPDiaAve^2) + I(BPDiaAve^3), data = nhanes09) 

summary(qtm, digits = 3)

## Call:

## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

## Multiple R-squared:  0.2398, Adjusted R-squared:  0.2396 
## F-statistic:  1218 on 2 and 7722 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
confint(qtm, level = 0.95)
##                      2.5 %       97.5 %
## (Intercept)   121.33361991 130.49457719
## BPDiaAve       -1.10466930  -0.81907630

summary(ctm, digits = 3)

confint(ctm, level = 0.95)

  1. Plot the training data along with the linear, quadratic and cubic fit lines in different colors.
# Store fitted values
linear_fit <- training_model$fitted.values
quad_fit <- qtm$fitted.values
cubic_fit <- ctm$fitted.values

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(nhanes09, aes(x = BPDiaAve, y = BPSysAve)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = BPSysAve), size = 0.5, alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = linear_fit, color = "Linear")) + 
  geom_line(aes(y = quad_fit, color = "Quadratic")) + 
  geom_line(aes(y = cubic_fit, color = "Cubic")) +
  labs(title = "Linear Model Fits Training Data",color = "Model Type", 
       x = "BPDiaAve", y = "BPSysAve") +
  theme_minimal()

  1. Which would be your preferred model based on the visual fits?

The linear model would be my preferred model based on the visual fit as it captures the general trend of the data, although the quadratic and cubic models capture the steeper slopes of the data better.

  1. Perform an anova test comparing the 3 models. Does the result seem in line with what you were expecting from the visual fits? Why/why not?
anova(training_model, qtm, ctm)
## Analysis of Variance Table
## 
## Model 1: BPSysAve ~ BPDiaAve
## Model 2: BPSysAve ~ BPDiaAve + I(BPDiaAve^2)
## Model 3: BPSysAve ~ BPDiaAve + I(BPDiaAve^2) + I(BPDiaAve^3)
##   Res.Df     RSS Df Sum of Sq       F    Pr(>F)    
## 1   7723 2130311                                   
## 2   7722 2008806  1    121505 468.336 < 2.2e-16 ***
## 3   7721 2003134  1      5672  21.864 2.976e-06 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

The results are not in line with what I expected, as adding the quadratic term significantly improved the model’s fit (F(1,1)) = 468.37, p <0.001) and explains more variance in BPSysAve than the linear model.

  1. Now plot BPSysAve against BPDiaAve for the test data and overlay the fitted linear, quadratic, and cubic models.
# Store predictions for test data
linear_pred <- predict(training_model, newdata = nhanes11)
quad_pred <- predict(qtm, newdata = nhanes11)
cubic_pred <- predict(ctm, newdata = nhanes11)

# Create dataframe for plotting
plot_data <- data.frame(
  BPDiaAve = nhanes11$BPDiaAve,
  BPSysAve = nhanes11$BPSysAve,
  linear_pred = linear_pred,
  quad_pred = quad_pred,
  cubic_pred = cubic_pred
)

# Plot
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = BPDiaAve)) + 
  geom_point(aes(y = BPSysAve), size = 0.5, alpha = 0.3) + 
  geom_line(aes(y = linear_pred, color = "Linear")) + 
  geom_line(aes(y = quad_pred, color = "Quadratic")) + 
  geom_line(aes(y = cubic_pred, color = "Cubic")) +
  labs(title = "Linear Model Fits Test Data", color = "Model Type",
       x = "BPDiaAve",
       y = "BPSysAve") +
  theme_minimal()

  1. Does this change your opinion at all about which is the best fit? Why/why not?

Yes, it changes my opinion about the best fit because I see the quadratic model captures how the relationship between BPDiaAve and BPSysAve becomes steeper as BPDiaAve increases. However, at lower values of BPDiaAve (>=50), the quadratic model shows a negative relationship between BPDiaAve and BPSysAve, which could be a model artifact or a fitting issue, which could impact the model’s clinical interpretability.

  1. Fit a nearest neighbors curve with ksmooth using the “normal” kernel to the nhanes09 data with bandwidths of 3, 10, and 20.
ksmooth3 <- ksmooth(nhanes09$BPDiaAve,nhanes09$BPSysAve, bandwidth = 3, kernel = "normal")
ksmooth10 <- ksmooth(nhanes09$BPDiaAve, nhanes09$BPSysAve, bandwidth = 10, kernel = "normal") 
ksmooth20 <- ksmooth(nhanes09$BPDiaAve, nhanes09$BPSysAve, bandwidth = 20, kernel = "normal")
  1. Plot the test data as well as the fitted curves from kernel smoothing and the best model fitted in the previous section using linear regression. Use different colors for each model.
# Store approximations for test data 
ksmooth_pred_3 <- approx(x = ksmooth3$x, y = ksmooth3$y, xout = nhanes11$BPDiaAve)$y
ksmooth_pred_10 <- approx(x = ksmooth10$x, y = ksmooth10$y, xout = nhanes11$BPDiaAve)$y
ksmooth_pred_20 <- approx(x = ksmooth20$x, y = ksmooth20$y, xout = nhanes11$BPDiaAve)$y

# Create dataframe for plotting 
plot_ksmooth <- data.frame(
  BPDiaAve = nhanes11$BPDiaAve,
  BPSysAve = nhanes11$BPSysAve,
  smooth_3 = ksmooth_pred_3,
  smooth_10 = ksmooth_pred_10,
  smooth_20 = ksmooth_pred_20
)

# Plot
ggplot(plot_ksmooth, aes(x = BPDiaAve)) + 
  geom_point(aes(y = BPSysAve), size = 0.5, alpha = 0.3) + 
  geom_line(aes(y = smooth_3, color = "Bandwidth 3")) + 
  geom_line(aes(y = smooth_10, color = "Bandwidth 10")) + 
  geom_line(aes(y = smooth_20, color = "Bandwidth 20")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = predict(qtm, newdata = nhanes11), color = "Best Model (Quadtratic)")) +
  labs(title = "Kernel Smoothing Test Data", color = "Model Type",
       x = "BPDiaAve",
       y = "BPSysAve") +
  theme_minimal()

  1. Based on the above results, which model would you pick? In the next section, we’ll evaluate the model based on its test error.

Based on the above results, I would pick the ksmooth model with a bandwidth of 10 as the as this fit line is closest to the quadratic fit line, which was evaluated to be the best model. However, if I had to choose between the ksmooth model with a bandwidth of 10 vs. the quadratic model, I would still chose the quadratic model.

Evaluating error on a test set

  1. Evaluate the mean squared error of the fitted models from the “Linear Regression” section on the test data. Also provide standard errors.
mse <- function(actual, predicted) {
  mean((actual - predicted)^2)
}

se_mse <- function(actual, predicted) {
  squared_errors <- (actual - predicted)^2
  sd(squared_errors)/sqrt(length(squared_errors))
}

mse_linear <- mse(nhanes11$BPSysAve, linear_pred)
mse_quadratic <- mse(nhanes11$BPSysAve, quad_pred)
mse_cubic <- mse(nhanes11$BPSysAve, cubic_pred)

se_linear <- se_mse(nhanes11$BPSysAve, linear_pred)
se_quadratic <- se_mse(nhanes11$BPSysAve, quad_pred)
se_cubic <- se_mse(nhanes11$BPSysAve, cubic_pred)

cat("Mean Squared Error (+- SE): \n",
    "Linear Model:", round(mse_linear, 4), "+-", round(se_linear, 4), "\n",
    "Quadratic Model:", round(mse_quadratic, 4), "+-", round(se_quadratic, 4), "\n",
    "Cubic Model:", round(mse_cubic, 4), "+-", round(se_cubic, 4), "\n")
## Mean Squared Error (+- SE): 
##  Linear Model: 266.9633 +- 7.2509 
##  Quadratic Model: 249.9912 +- 6.9218 
##  Cubic Model: 250.0889 +- 6.9263
  1. Using ANOVA, did we pick the model with the lowest mean squared error on the test data? Why do you think this happened?

Yes, using ANOVA, we picked the model with the lowest mean squared error on the test data. This happened because ANOVA identified the model with the lowest p-value and highest F-statistic, which reflects a high explained variance (numerator), relative to a low residual variance (denominator). The low mean squared error is a consequence of the low residual variance as the equations for the residual variance (denominator of F-statistic) and the MSE for the predictors is the same, except for the adjustment of (n-p) vs just n in the denominator.

  1. Evaluate the mean squared error of the fitted models from kernel smoothing on the test data.
mse_ksmooth_3 <- mse(nhanes11$BPSysAve, ksmooth_pred_3)
mse_ksmooth_10 <- mse(nhanes11$BPSysAve, ksmooth_pred_10)
mse_ksmooth_20 <- mse(nhanes11$BPSysAve, ksmooth_pred_20)

cat("Mean Squared Error: \n",
    "Bandwith 3:", round(mse_ksmooth_3, 4), "\n",
    "Bandwith 10:", round(mse_ksmooth_10, 4), "\n",
    "Bandwith 20:", round(mse_ksmooth_20, 4), "\n")
## Mean Squared Error: 
##  Bandwith 3: 250.1672 
##  Bandwith 10: 250.1062 
##  Bandwith 20: 256.4335
  1. Among all the methods we tried, which one had the lowest test error?

Among all the methods we tried, the quadratic model had the lowest test error with MSE: 249.9912 ± 6.9218 and RMSE: √249.9912 ≈ 15.81 mmHg, indicating an average deviation of 15.81 mmHg between predicted and actual BPSysAve values.
